newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Stoyanov predicts run-off win.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Stoyanov predicts run-off win.

text.p: Opposition leader Petar Stoyanov claimed victory in the first round of Bulgaria's presidential election on Sunday and predicted he would win next weekend's run-off.

Unofficial projections based on early results showed the 44-year-old lawyer had comfortably beaten Socialist government candidate Ivan Marazov into second place but had failed to win an absolute majority.

Stoyanov hailed the vote as a sea-change in voting patterns among Bulgaria's 6.75 million electorate, most of whom have seen their living standards slump under the Socialists since the fall of communism in 1989.
"The vote shows that a new majority is being formed," he told a news conference. "Half of it supported the new and reasonable programme represented by me."
The other half, he said, had "chosen the path of complete negativity" by voting for the third-placed George Ganchev, head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc.
"I expect them to vote for me in the second round," Stoyanov added.

Several projections issued by independent polling groups agreed that Stoyanov, vice-chairman of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), had won between 43 and 46 percent of the vote, still short of the 50 percent he needed to win outright.
The Socialist Marazov had 23 to 28 percent, with Ganchev just a percentage point or two behind.
Final results were expected on Monday morning.
Official estimates showed some 60 percent of the 6.75 million electorate in this former Soviet satellite had turned out to vote.
Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov has a secure majority in parliament -- where real power in Bulgaria lies -- but the UDF currently holds the more ceremonial post of president.
Stoyanov said one of his first acts if elected on November 3 would be to ask Videnov to reveal the full extent of the country's economic crisis.
"I will be pressing him to come forward with concrete solutions," he added.

Political analysts have also forecast that a big rebuff for the ex-communist Socialists will widen rifts within their ranks that have become more public since the still unsolved October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Parliament is only half way through its four-year term but cabinet changes are a possibility, they said.
The reform laggard of the ex-Warsaw Pact east European countries, this largely agricultural nation of just 8.4 million people has been slow to shake off its communist legacy.
While most other ex-Soviet states have seen some benefits from economic reform and are pressing for inclusion in NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria remains mired in its post-war legacy.

An ambitious privatisation programme remains largely stalled in the face of powerful vested interests while several foreign investors privately complain Sofia still looks more to Moscow for inspiration than Brussels.
Prices are rising, the unit of currency, the lev, is falling, the central interest rate is 240 percent and foreign exchange reserves have plunged to about $505 million from $1.5 billion a year ago.
